vignette:
Arun used to say the forest spoke to him. For fifteen years as a park ranger, the snap of a twig, the rustle of leaves, the call of a distant hawk were all part of a familiar language. He knew the park's secrets-where the deer bedded down at dusk, which ancient oaks were most likely to drop limbs in a storm. The vast, open wilderness was his sanctuary, the place where he felt most himself, most in control. That was before the incident on the western ridge.

It was a routine patrol, nearly two years ago now. He'd been tracking what he thought were poachers, but he stumbled onto something far more organized: an illegal grow operation, tucked deep in a ravine. He barely had time to reach for his radio before he was surrounded. They were armed, their faces hard. They took his radio, his phone, his sidearm, and bound his hands with zip ties that bit deep into his wrists. For three days, they kept him in a small, damp shed. The world shrank to the smell of mildew and unwashed bodies, the rough texture of the burlap sack they'd sometimes throw over his head, and the muffled sound of their voices deciding what to do with him. He remembers the cold, metallic feel of a gun barrel pressed against his temple and the chillingly calm voice that said, "You saw nothing. You are nothing." On the third night, they drove him miles away, shoved him out of a truck, and disappeared. He walked for hours before finding a familiar trail.

When he was found, everyone called him a hero, a survivor. His partner, Priya, held him, and his colleagues slapped him on the back. He tried to wear the title, but it felt like a costume. He went back to work a month later, telling everyone he was fine, that he just wanted to get back to normal. But the language of the forest had changed. The snap of a twig was no longer a deer; it was a footstep behind him. The rustle of leaves was no longer the wind; it was someone waiting.

Now, at 41, Arun rarely patrols the deep woods. He sticks to the well-trodden paths near the visitor center, his hand hovering near his hip. His eyes, once trained to spot a rare bird or the subtle track of a bobcat, now scan the tree line for things that are out of place, for threats that aren't there. He feels a constant, low-grade hum of anxiety, a coiled spring in his gut that tightens whenever a hiker with a large backpack appears unexpectedly on the trail. He tells himself he is being vigilant, but he knows it is fear.

At home, the walls of his small house feel like they are closing in. He can't sleep through the night, often waking up in a cold sweat, the phantom sensation of zip ties tight around his wrists. He startles at the sound of the ice maker, the slam of a car door down the street. Priya tries to reach him, her touch gentle, her questions soft. But he feels a chasm between them. He'll sit on the couch, staring at the television without seeing it, the silence of the room more deafening than any noise. Sometimes, her attempts to comfort him feel like a cage, and a flash of anger, hot and unfamiliar, will rise in him. He'll snap at her over nothing-a misplaced set of keys, a question asked at the wrong time. He immediately regrets it, but the shame only builds the wall between them higher. He feels weak, a fraud in the ranger uniform that once felt like a second skin. He looks out his window at the familiar peaks of the mountains he once loved, but they no longer look like a sanctuary. They look like walls.
